title: Unseen, Unfair, Unscripted
subtitle: Field Notes No. 004 · Stealth routes, manipulation and traps
rightsNotice: Game images and quoted material belong to their respective rights holders. Included for commentary and criticism; no endorsement or ownership is implied.
editorial: Field Notes No. 004 is about games that let you win dishonestly. Not by cheating, but by reading people: noticing where a guard looks, what he eats, who he works for, and which floor tile he's about to step on. Tenchu: Stealth Assassins is where to start. It's the 1998 PlayStation original, with one gauge and ten missions, and its Western release is actually more complete than the Japanese one. Metal Gear Solid 3: Subsistence turns survival into stealth tools: camouflage you manage by percentage, food you can poison, and bosses you can outwait instead of outfight. Shinobido: Way of the Ninja, from the original Tenchu team, hands you a three-sided war and lets your contracts decide who wins. Deception III: Dark Delusion turns the whole idea around: you're the one being invaded, and the building is your only weapon. Each article names the edition it describes, because here the edition matters: an extra two missions, a third disc, an English dub, a disc that never left North America. Edition details, reviews and control advice come from the cited manuals, reviews, databases and fan guides, and each article separates what those sources say from our own judgement and inference. None of these games was played for this issue. Four short warnings, one per game: Tenchu ignores the analog stick; Subsistence relies on pressure-sensitive buttons; Shinobido's camera was unpopular even in 2006; and Deception III's 2000 translation was widely mocked.

articles.deck: The 1998 original that made a single awareness gauge the whole game. The North American release is the expanded Western cut, with ten missions and three random layouts each. Here's what changed from Japan, how the ranks pay you back, and why the D-pad is your only controller.

articles.deck: Acquire's PS2 ninja game never reached North America. The European disc is the friendlier edition, with subtitles and a Japanese voice option. Three factions post contracts, and every job you take shifts the war. The camera is as bad as reviewers said; the system underneath is worth the fight.
articles.imageCaption: Goh crouches at the foot of a wooden bridge at night while a guard crosses at right; the eye icon at top centre tracks enemy awareness and the compass at top right points toward the nearest guard. PAL PS2 screenshot © Acquire / Spike Chunsoft, via ScreenScraper.

articles.deck: Tecmo's 1999 trap game puts you on the defending side. Set ceiling, wall and floor traps, chain them into fifteen-hit combos, and build new traps from parts. It was probably never released in Europe: here's which disc to look for and what its split 2000 reviews got right.
articles.imageCaption: A Mega Rock ceiling trap rolls over the soldier Jade in the Chapter I dungeon, scoring 50 damage. Frame from ScreenScraper's gameplay video of the US release; © Tecmo / Koei Tecmo.
